newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibian economy set to grow by five pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Namibian economy set to grow by five pct in 1997.

text.p: The Namibian economy performed better than expected last year raising hopes of a growth rate of five percent in 1997, the independent Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit (NEPRU) said in its March quarterly review.
It said that the three percent growth rate in 1996 was mainly due to a significant boost in the agricultural sector despite harsh drought conditions.
Farmers were forced to increase the slaughter of livestock last year because of the drought and poor grazing conditions.

"Five percent is quite possible. Unfortunately in Namibia growth depends on facts which are beyond government's control such as the weather, but if we had three percent growth even in a drought year it should be quite possible to achieve more in a normal year," senior NEPRU researcher, Dirk Hansohm said.
Drought conditions have eased somewhat this year after good rains.
"Total agricultural output for 1996 was approximately 10 to 15 percent higher than in the previous year and this should contribute to an increase in overall output," NEPRU said.
The report showed a slight drop in inflation at the end of 1996 to 8.45 percent in December from 8.6 percent in November, a trend which began with the currency's depreciation a year ago.
The NEPRU said inflationary pressure should ease with the stabilisation of the Namibian dollar.

The research body however noted that the closely linked interest rates of South Africa and Namibia remained high with the prime rate in Namibia now at 21 percent, but it predicted a slight drop in rates in the first half of 1997.

"Stabilisation of the South African rand is an important precondition for cuts in interest rates, and this is likely to lead to a one percent reduction in South Africa during the first six months of this year, with Namibia closely following," the body concluded.
NEPRU cautioned the government to diversify its revenue sources more as there was too much reliance on receipts from the Southern African Customs Union (SACU).
"In the long term our problem is the high dependence on the SACU revenue pool and I think Namibia cannot hope to get higher revenues from the renegotiation of the agreement," Hansohm said.
"In the face of trade liberalisation we expect that revenue from tariffs to decline, so we have to go more for other taxes -- direct and indirect," he added.
Finance Minister Nangolo Mbumba said in his budget speech earlier this month that SACU revenue has become the largest single tax category in Namibia.
NEPRU also highlighted good results by the Namibian Stock Exchange last year with a three-fold increase of share trading reaching a total value of N$660.5 million.
It said the trend is set to continue given recent announcements of major companies listing on the NSE such as Namdeb and First National Bank Namibia.
